draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Belur! This was the first capital of the Hoysala kings, and its Chennakeshava Temple took 103 years and three generations to build. Since 2023 it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
draft.hungryLine: Eat like the Hassan locals with ragi mudde and avarekaalina saaru, or some tangy puliyogare, and finish with a proper coffee.

moodReplies.show-me-around: The Chennakesava Temple is just a 6 min walk, and the little Kappe Chennigaraya Temple is right beside it in the same complex.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Take your time with the carvings inside the temple complex, especially Darpana Sundari, the lady with the mirror.
moodReplies.surprise-me: The mineral beryl, and so beryllium, is named after Belur.

tips.title: Mind the sanctum breaks.
tips.body: The inner sanctum closes 10AM-11AM, 1PM-3PM and 5PM-5:30PM, so plan your darshan around that.

tips.title: Take guide stories lightly.
tips.body: Government-approved guides are handy, but some of what they tell you is made up, so enjoy it with a pinch of salt.

story.title: A king's temple
story.body: King Vishnuvardhana commissioned the Chennakeshava Temple on the banks of the Yagachi River. Belur was then the first capital of the Hoysalas, before they built Dwarasamudra, today's Halebidu.

story.title: 103 years of carving
story.body: The temple took three generations to finish. Its soapstone walls show 12th-century life, dancers and musicians, and scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

story.title: The gravity pillar
story.body: A 42 foot lamp post pillar was put up in the temple complex in 1414. It's still standing today.

story.title: Siege of Belur
story.body: In the last years of the Vijayanagara Empire, Shivappa Nayaka of Keladi besieged Belur to back Emperor Sriranga III. He won and restored the emperor's authority here.

story.title: World Heritage
story.body: The Hoysala monuments at Belur and Halebidu became UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Poojas have been done here every morning and evening since the 12th century.
